title: Limitations of Soup2nuts Ai: Postmortem
author: PerformanceProud1252
selftext:
I wanted to explore the boundaries of what was possible with soup to nuts Ai development by intentionally stress testing a couple models. No game engine. Just pure code.

Here is a break down of the process and cost.

The game: A brand new TCG where players fight for a beacon to bring back to home base.

1. First I asked Sol 5.6 Max Effort to generate the rules of the TCG. I asked for originality and got it.  
2. Then I asked it to develop a well balanced set of 300 cards with unique abilities, traits, and stats.  
3. Afterwards, I asked for 20 unique deck lists. The model excelled at these tasks. And went above and beyond by  creating themed decks with different goals/strategies.  
4. I fed the specs into Grok 4.6. It built the original game scaffolding for about $10 but completely failed to generate a passable Ui. It used Babylon.js, and vite. What I was impressed by was it handled thousands of card ability edge cases and implemented a rules-based Ai to play against.  
5. I switched to Opus 5 to audit Grok’s code and to develop a good Ui. It seems to have a better sense of taste. Overall, this cost about $200 in tokens.  
6. A mostly playable game with a polished Ui that has a few bugs. Those last 1% of bugs weren’t worth the compute and I had to drop the project.

Unfortunately the game was not fun to play. Most of the abilities frankly don’t matter and you can play without them. Still, I was blown away with the amount of complexity these models could handle. Overall, I still recommend Sol 5.6 for the cost and performance.
